title: The mayor and Montaigne
hook: elected mayor of Bordeaux, he says the mayor and Montaigne were always two (Essays 3.10)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Montaigne travels, and your line was a new route. Did a different turn show you something you'd never noticed? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-seven.

The man who walked away from public life to sit in a tower with his books gets called back. The city of Bordeaux elects him mayor. Montaigne takes the job. And then, in an essay of book three about how to manage your own will, he says something that sounds almost like a riddle: the mayor and Montaigne have always been two, clearly separated. Same body, same signature, same house. Two. What could that mean, and why would anyone want it?
screen: `BORDEAUX CALLS HIM BACK.` → `HE TAKES THE JOB.` → `THE MAYOR AND MONTAIGNE: TWO.`

segments.voice: First, the role as a part in a play. Montaigne says we should play our part well, but as a part, a borrowed character. The mask is real and the work is real, but the mask is not the face. He warns against people who let the office soak into them, who become their title all the way down, and carry it home to the dinner table. Second, how deep the job goes. He's willing, he says, to take the city's affairs into his hands, but not into his lungs and liver. He'll carry the work; he won't let it eat him. That's not laziness. It's a way of staying clear enough to do the work well. Third, the critics. He admits some people said his time as mayor left little mark, that he was too easygoing. He doesn't hide it. He answers that he kept things calm, did no harm, and didn't stir up trouble just to look busy. Readers can judge whether that's enough. But he's honest about the trade he chose. Fourth, why two matters. When the role and the person are fused, every attack on the work feels like an attack on the self, and every loss of the job feels like a loss of who you are. When they're two, you can give the role your best and still go home as yourself. Today, the role might be manager, nurse, parent on duty, the one who always fixes things. Do it fully. Then take off the badge.
screen: `PLAY THE PART AS A PART.` · `IN THE HANDS, NOT THE LIVER.` · `HONEST ABOUT HIS CRITICS.` · `GIVE YOUR BEST, GO HOME AS YOU.` · then, large: `TWO, NOT ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep your role and yourself apart. Sit, and let the breath slow. Name one role you carry: at work, at home, in your family or your town. Picture it as a coat you wear. Notice how it sits on your shoulders, what it asks of you, what you're proud of in it. Now, for this sit, imagine hanging the coat on a hook by the door. It will be there when you need it. Underneath is just you, breathing. Stay with that person for a while. The bell holds the time.
The mayor and Montaigne. A role worn fully, and a self kept distinct underneath it. Today's word.
Your line: two, not one. Today, when you finish a task for your role, pause at the door and say it: two, not one. Then walk in as yourself. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often quote his line that the mayor and Montaigne were always two as a picture of doing a public role fully while keeping the self distinct from it.
